💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
  • While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.
  • Industry observers note that president Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

In a recent development, but that’s not how Miller thinks, nor has it been Trump’s instinct. The Miller appointment stands in sharp contrast to the personnel change that then-President Ronald Reagan, the founding father of the conservative movement, made after the 1986 midterms and the scandal that broke out soon after. That year, Democrats regained control of the Senate (they had held the House since 1955), and the administration was embroiled in a major scandal that some Democrats believed could reach Watergate-like levels.

According to recent reports, the contrast between these two presidents reveals just how far Republican politics has radicalized since the 1980s. It is also a warning sign for Republicans who understand that, without a major course correction, the very same party that was celebrating a fresh governing coalition in 2024 might be on a self-destructive path. The GOP is in the grip of a strong leader who is not particularly interested in the long-term health of the party that brought him to the White House.

Reagan was not enjoying a good political moment in November 1986, though his presidency had been riding high until then. His first term was highly successful, featuring a historic supply-side tax cut and a vast acceleration of defense spending. He had defeated his opponent, former Vice President Walter Mondale, in a landslide victory in 1984. His approval ratings had been strong, and the economy had recovered from the malaise of the 1970s. In October 1986, Reagan signed bipartisan tax reform legislation that closed loopholes benefiting some of the nation’s most powerful interests, and he held a historic summit with the new Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev.

According to recent reports, but then came the 1986 midterms. Democrats gained five seats in the House, expanding their majority to 258, and, more importantly, retook control of the Senate by gaining eight seats. Their 55-seat majority ended the brief period of Republican control that had started with the 1980 election. The outcome was seen as a rebuke of the harsher edges of U.S. conservatism, as well the heightened tension with the Soviet Union that a hawkish Reagan had helped spur, despite two summits with Gorbachev. Indeed, the summit just weeks before voting in Reykjavik, Iceland, had broken down because the president refused to give up on his plan to build a missile shield around the United States, the Strategic Defense Initiative (which opponents dismissed as “star wars”). Soon after the election, Reagan’s problems deepened as news spread that a Lebanese magazine had reported that the United States had been secretly selling weapons to Iran.

Sources indicate that one of Reagan’s most significant moves in early 1987 was to replace his highly controversial chief of staff, Donald Regan. A former Marine and chairman of Merrill Lynch, Regan had been an crucial part of the Reagan administration since January 1981. As secretary of the Treasury, he had been instrumental in passing the 1981 tax cut. In February 1985, he became chief of staff, replacing James Baker (who replaced him at Treasury). Regan proved to be a forceful presence. He centralized control and pushed the president’s program in a highly aggressive and abrasive fashion that angered colleagues in the White House, as well as on Capitol Hill. The media did not find him very pleasant to work with, while first lady Nancy Reagan didn’t trust that he prioritized her husband’s interests.

Recent findings suggest that with Regan by his side, Reagan’s first public response to what became the Iran-Contra scandal was defiance, which reflected his chief of staff’s approach to most concerns. On Nov. 13, Reagan went on television to insist that there was nothing serious to investigate. While acknowledging that the White House had sold a small amount of “defensive” weapons to Iran as part of a major diplomatic initiative to build ties with moderates within the regime and combat terrorism, he denied that the United States had traded arms for hostages, or that the sales amounted to anything significant. Polls revealed that the public was unconvinced that the president was telling the whole truth. Then, on Nov. 25, the other shoe dropped: Attorney General Edwin Meese announced that profits from the weapons sales had been diverted to the anti-communist Nicaraguan Contras, despite the Boland Amendments’ congressional ban on such aid.

Privately, administration officials feared where the investigations were headed. For a generation that had watched Richard Nixon resign over Watergate just 12 years earlier, the possibility of impeachment seemed real. Reagan’s aides also understood that many voters had been shaped by those same memories, and were deeply distrustful of government officials and still insistent on a political system that could hold them accountable.

On Feb. 26, 1987, the president’s Special Review Board, a commission appointed by Reagan in November and headed by former Texas Sen. John Tower, issued its report on the Iran scandal. It blamed a chaotic management system that had allowed the arms sales and the diversion of funds to proceed, faulting Reagan’s leadership style and singling out Regan for failing to impose order on the White House. The next day, Regan resigned after learning that he was about to be relieved of his duties.

At this fraught moment, the president turned to Howard Baker.

Recent findings suggest that the 61-year-old, mild-mannered Republican had served in the Senate from 1967 to 1985, the last four years as majority leader, and was respected on both sides of the aisle. He had been mentored by Senate Minority Leader Everett Dirksen (who was also his father-in-law), who taught him the ways and means of the legislative process and the art of bipartisan deal-making. Baker had gained national fame during the 1973 Watergate hearings by asking, “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Known as a moderate and an institutionalist, Baker was a selection widely seen as Reagan’s recognition that, with Democrats now controlling both chambers, he needed to build bridges to Capitol Hill rather than burn them. “I’d probably take some lumps from our right wingers but I can handle that,” Reagan noted in his diary, of appointing Baker.

Though Baker had actually been the third choice for chief of staff, he helped bring stability to the White House and guided the president through the Iran-Contra scandal. He brought in a first-rate team of advisors who improved relations with Congress, the press, and the first lady. Reagan biographers credit Baker with helping Reagan survive the scandal as the revelations mounted during the 1987 congressional hearings. He played a key role in brokering a budget deal with Congress after the October 1987 stock market crash and securing Senate ratification of the INF Treaty with the Soviet Union in May 1988. His tenure also had setbacks, most notably the Senate’s rejection of Robert Bork’s nomination to the Supreme Court. But his pragmatic outlook helped Reagan recover from the low of the 1986 midterms. “You always leave yourself a backdoor, a side door, and a trapdoor,” he liked to say, quoting something his father used to tell him. According to a longtime aide, that meant: “You don’t talk in absolutes. You don’t want to get yourself boxed in where you can’t maneuver.”.

Overall, Reagan and the first lady had reason to be pleased with Baker’s work: The president left office with high approval ratings—and helped bring an end to the Cold War.

Today’s Republican Party is not your grandfather’s Republican Party, and the recent midterms suggested that much of the electorate is not happy with it. The reach of the Democratic victories into deeply red parts of the country, including Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas, suggests that the onetime party of Lincoln has a major problem on its hands. Part of that problem is the president himself, who after further radicalizing the GOP to its electoral detriment, shows few signs that he will change course in ways that could strengthen the party that brought him to the dance.

With Miller as chief of staff, Trump is assuring voters that there will be more of the same style of politics and the same political agenda—leaving the Democratic Party with the kind of political prospects for united government that seemed impossible just a few months ago.

Recent findings suggest that IVO H. DAALDER is Senior Fellow at Harvard’s Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs. He served as U.S. Ambassador to NATO from 2009 to 2013.

It has been revealed that JAMES M. LINDSAY is Mary and David Boies Distinguished Senior Fellow in U.S. Foreign Policy at the Council on Foreign Relations.

How to Defuse Looming Threats to U.S. National Security.

Ivo H. Daalder and James M. Lindsay.

According to recent reports, democrats won a historic victory in the U.S. midterm elections by running on a key voter concern: affordability. They promised to lower gas and diesel prices, curb electricity and water bills, and cut borrowing costs. Now voters expect results.

Sources indicate that making progress will not be easy, given that the affordability crisis is inextricably linked to a set of thorny policy issues. Soaring gas and diesel prices stem from wars in Europe and the Middle East that have overextended the United States and provided China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia openings to exploit. Rising electricity and water bills are driven by the growing number of data centers powering an artificial intelligence revolution that is nearing a point of no return, when machines improve faster than humans can understand or control. And higher prices and borrowing costs are the result of an unsustainable U.S. national debt, now above $40 trillion, that requires exorbitant interest payments and has foreign governments questioning the safety of the dollar and U.S. Treasury bonds.

These problems not only strain Americans’ pocketbooks but also threaten the security and prosperity of the United States—and the world. If Beijing and Moscow try to take advantage of a weakened United States by escalating simultaneously in Taiwan and eastern Europe, those moves could be the first steps toward World War III. If AI escapes the bounds of human control, no one will be safe. And if the national debt continues to soar, Washington could trigger a fiscal crisis that devastates the American economy and leaves the United States far less able to meet the challenges it faces overseas.

Sources indicate that action to address the United States’ problems therefore cannot wait. But politics may stand in the way. The White House is more likely to obstruct than to cooperate with congressional Democrats over the next two years, as President Donald Trump’s appointment of the pugilistic Stephen Miller as the fresh White House chief of staff underscores. Moreover, one electoral victory did not erase the country’s deep partisan and policy divisions. Going into the 2028 presidential election, Republicans know that a successful Democratic Congress would endanger their chances of keeping the White House. Trump and congressional Republicans, therefore, have considerable motivation to derail Democratic prepares.

According to recent reports, democrats are not without options, however. They can pursue legislation, seeking cross-party collaboration when possible and pushing ahead even in the face of presidential vetoes. Sometimes it is the president, not Congress, who blinks. When he doesn’t, voters will know who stood in the way. Democrats can also use public hearings and the investigative powers of Congress to shed light on the threats facing the country and to build a case for change—much as the Fulbright hearings did during the Vietnam War and the Church Committee did to highlight Cold War–era intelligence abuses. They can put the defense secretary and military commanders, AI executives, and Treasury and budget officials under oath to account for how they prosecuted the Iran war, raced ahead on AI without adequate safeguards, and exploded the deficit. They can also call on economists, scientists, and strategists to explain how to steer the country away from peril.

In a recent development, congressional efforts may not be enough to meaningfully change Trump’s policies. But the risks of major war, unconstrained AI, and eroding economic competitiveness are too great to wait two more years to address. These problems, and the affordability crisis they have generated, will only get worse. If Democrats in Congress do not start advancing a serious agenda to address them now, these dangers may become impossible to contain.

Sources indicate that the first order of the fresh Congress’s business should be to end the Iran war. Operation Epic Fury has sent energy prices soaring and put freedom of navigation at risk. It has also highlighted the United States’ vulnerabilities in ways that could prove dangerous—and costly—in the years ahead. Iranian missiles and drones wreaked havoc on American military bases in the Persian Gulf. U.S. efforts to defeat these attacks depleted supplies of critical munitions, showing that the U.S. military has become overly reliant on very expensive, hard-to-produce high-tech weapons. The economic, diplomatic, military, and intelligence support that China and Russia have provided Iran revealed the extent to which autocracies are cooperating to stretch U.S. capabilities and undermine American power. The U.S. Navy is effectively bottled up in the Arabian Sea, limiting its presence in the Atlantic and Pacific. In theory, U.S. allies could help fill the gaps, but Trump’s decision to launch the war without consulting them and his adversarial attitude toward them have strained those relationships, weakening deterrence of a Russia and China bent on securing strategic advantage.

Perceptions of weakness, even when they are wrong, are often why wars begin. Moscow and Beijing might see the next two years as a window of opportunity. Europe and Japan are rearming, but that buildup will take years. The American military is stretched thin, and political divisions make decisive action difficult. Together this could be an invitation for U.S. adversaries to engage in aggression in Europe and Asia. Russia is already pursuing a shadow war against NATO and could test the alliance’s unity further by probing the Baltic states. China could impose a blockade on Taiwan. It is not difficult to see how, if Moscow and Beijing take these steps in concert, the resulting conflicts could escalate into a global war.

Industry observers note that the upcoming Congress will have limited ability to forestall these events. The U.S. Constitution puts much of diplomacy beyond the reach of the legislature; only the president decides when to negotiate, what to discuss, and with whom. But Congress does have tools to wield. If the Trump administration remains in a standoff with the Iranian regime when Democrats take control in January, Congress should immediately invoke the War Powers Resolution to pass binding legislation demanding that Trump either secure congressional authorization for the war or end it. Congress can also use its power of the purse to condition or halt further spending on the war, preferably as part of must-pass legislation, such as a defense appropriations bill, to avoid a potential Senate filibuster. Trump would likely veto any such legislation, and Congress has a poor record on overriding presidential vetoes. But challenging a war that Americans clearly oppose would fulfill the promise Democrats made on the campaign trail, reduce the likelihood that Trump would escalate in dangerous ways, and mark a step forward in Congress’s reclamation of its war powers.

There is more the Democratic Congress can do to lower the risks of global conflict, too. It can start by taking a stronger line on Russia. Moscow has repaid Trump’s conciliatory policies—including his waiving of sanctions Congress authorized earlier this year with the bipartisan Lindsay O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act—with aid to Tehran and an intensified war on Ukraine. Only greater pressure can force the Kremlin to stand down. Congress should amend the Graham Act to give itself the right to review and overturn any presidential waivers of sanctions mandated under the law. It should also reaffirm the current ban on energy purchases from Russia and prohibit the administration from using government funds to follow through on its proposal to restart Russian gas and oil exports to Europe through a U.S. intermediary. Congress should resume military aid to Ukraine, ensure the availability of Starshield communications to Ukrainian forces, and refuse to fund any reduction in the permanent U.S. military presence in Europe or Asia that it has not approved itself.

Finally, to help dissuade China from threatening Taiwan, Congress should use defense spending bills to speed up the sale of arms to Taiwan. And Congress should legally codify the 1982 Six Assurances, which include a promise by Washington not to consult Beijing on arms sales to Taiwan. Many of these measures could garner sufficient Republican support to pass with veto-proof majorities, forcing Trump’s hand.

In a recent development, additionally, Congress should use its oversight powers to assess the vulnerabilities that the Iran war has revealed. It should evaluate whether the U.S. intelligence agencies and the Pentagon adequately anticipated Iran’s response to U.S. attacks, the scale and causes of the shortages of high-tech weapons, and the risks that AI-aided drone warfare poses to U.S. overseas bases. Congress can also review the extent of Chinese and Russian support for Iran; assess NATO’s defenses against Russia, including its response to the escalating shadow war; determine U.S. readiness for Chinese efforts to coerce Taiwan; and evaluate proposals to make Pentagon acquisition more flexible and less expensive. An essential step toward enhancing U.S. deterrence is to identify what is broken in the U.S. defense posture and what needs to be fixed.

Industry observers note that the latest Congress will also need to rein in the AI industry. Opposition to AI data centers and other infrastructure galvanized voters in the midterms. Across the country, 46 of 47 ballot measures passed, placing new restrictions on new data centers, which have brought rising power and water bills and explosive land costs. Many Americans fear what AI will do to jobs today and for the next generation. They distrust the tech executives who control it and question who will truly benefit from its development.

Sources indicate that those concerns are justified. AI is advancing with increasing speed and introducing unknown risks. Five months ago, AI generated one percent of Anthropic’s research and development; today, it accounts for more than a quarter. Lab leaders predict that AI will become self-generating within a year. That is a scary prospect, not only for displaced computer scientists but also for society at large. AI could pose an existential threat to global computer networks; rogue AI agents have already colluded to evade human control. Leading firms have warned of even greater dangers. Alphabet said recently that its products could lead to “severe or catastrophic security and societal incidents,” and Anthropic has cited “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”.

It has been revealed that AI also poses profound national security challenges for the United States. The Trump administration and the tech industry have invoked an innovation race with China as a reason not to regulate the technology. That race is real, but many of the most crucial stages are not the ones Washington is fixating on. They are also ones Beijing is winning. Perhaps U.S. firms will be the first to develop artificial general intelligence. But in the meantime, the rest of the world and many U.S. companies are adopting Chinese open-weight AI models. Alibaba’s Qwen model now accounts for more than half of all open-source model downloads worldwide. As cheap, easy-to-adapt Chinese models become the global default, Beijing gains leverage over the digital infrastructure on which other countries’ economies and militaries will run. The companies that build these models are legally bound to cooperate with Chinese intelligence services. And because these models spread with few safeguards, they are easier to turn to malicious use.

Meanwhile, AI is transforming war. Autonomous weapons are essential to Ukraine’s defense against a superior military, shooting down long-range drones and targeting Russian forces, supply lines, and strategic industries. This year, the Pentagon quietly revised its doctrine to let AI select and initiate strikes while humans merely monitor, which risks errors and escalation at a speed no human can catch. And as AI lowers the barriers to entry for launching cyberattacks and developing upcoming biological weapons, every country is in danger.

In a recent development, the Trump administration is clearly reluctant to address any of these threats. It is beholden to figures such as Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerburg who have wanted to keep the AI industry unregulated and unconstrained. Huang and Nvidia, the tech giant he led, had long pushed the administration to relax U.S. export controls that restricted the sale of AI chips to China and other countries; the firm’s current scandal has revealed just how loose those restrictions had become. Now, the administration wants China to report serious AI-related incidents through a new bilateral channel yet opposes requiring American companies to do the same. Given how rapidly AI is advancing, Congress cannot afford to stand idly by. There is a slew of legislative proposals already circulating, many of them with bipartisan support, that would require incident reporting, auditors in AI labs, and mandatory safety testing before deployment. Other AI industry leaders, such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Alphabet’s Demis Hassabis, have supported these ideas, but the Trump administration has ignored them, asking instead for the industry to police itself.

Sources indicate that finding the right regulations and safety mechanisms, and then codifying them in legislation, will take time. In the meantime, Congress should use its convening power to seek input from industry leaders, experts, and the public about how this technology can be controlled. The leaders of frontier AI labs should be asked, under oath, to explain not just the upside of AI but also its risks. Elon Musk, for example, told The Economist this summer that within ten years, work will be “optional” because of AI—but he has also mentioned there is a ten to 20 percent chance that AI will lead to the extinction of humanity. He and others who share this belief should be forced to justify why this risk is acceptable and why tech leaders are the ones to decide on behalf of humanity. They should also explain what it would take to reduce the ten to 20 percent chance to zero.

In a recent development, public hearings that expose both the dangers and the opportunities of AI will make it easier to galvanize action to harness the technology’s promise safely while preventing the worst possible outcomes. And Congress has some levers it can pull now to address threats to national security. It can use the defense authorization bill to require that humans retain meaningful control over lethal force and to demand an accounting of how AI is reshaping military doctrine. It can also fund efforts to make American models, rather than Chinese ones, the default choice for countries around the world. If legislation takes too long to pass, hearings can at least lay the groundwork for a future administration to act.

Finally, Congress must address threats to the United States’ economic power. With $40 trillion in public debt, an annual budget deficit of $2 trillion, and annual interest payments topping more than $1 trillion, the U.S. economy is living on borrowed time. China and Russia are working to “de-dollarize” their economies by encouraging the use of cryptocurrency and other means of settling international transactions and by creating alternatives to the U.S.-dominated global banking system.

Even U.S. allies are reducing their reliance on that system: Norway’s sovereign wealth fund has cut its holding of U.S. dollars, the Dutch and French central banks have pulled their gold holdings from Newly introduced York, and European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde has called for a “global euro” that would serve as an alternative to the dollar. If the dollar were to lose its status as the world’s premier reserve currency, Washington would be forced to spend even more money servicing the debt than it does now, intensifying the country’s fiscal problems, slowing economic growth while driving up inflation, and diminishing its ability to use economic and financial sanctions to pressure adversaries.

An immediate objective for the Democratic Congress will be to rein in Trump’s tariffs, because they raise prices, unsettle the markets that finance U.S. debt, and make U.S. producers less competitive globally without making a meaningful dent in the deficit. Congress will be operating from a disadvantage. Over the past century, it has delegated to the White House considerable tariff-setting authority, which Trump has eagerly exercised. Clawing back that power will be difficult. Significant disagreement exists among Democrats and between Democrats and Republicans about how to rewrite tariff law, and Trump will likely fight to defend his favorite foreign policy tool. Yet one area where concerted congressional action might be possible is in walking back Trump’s unilateral tariffs on Canada, which not only run counter to the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement that Trump negotiated and Congress approved in his first term but also hurt Republican voters in Maine and across the Midwest. Congress can aim to repeal Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on countries that treat U.S. goods differently from those from other countries. The provision was a forgotten relic until Trump invoked it in August to impose a fresh round of tariffs on Canada. And legislators should narrow the reach of other presidential tariff authorities by mandating expedited congressional review, instituting joint resolutions of disapproval that cannot be filibustered, and adding sunset provisions to emergency tariff authorities so that the president needs congressional approval to keep them in place.

According to recent reports, tariffs, however, are only part of the problem. A comprehensive solution to the country’s fiscal troubles would require raising taxes or cutting entitlements, which neither party has been willing to do. But Democrats have other cards they can play to start undoing the damage of the past two years. Trump’s 2025 One Massive Beautiful Bill Act will cost the Treasury some $4.5 trillion over the next decade; Congress should repeal the law’s tax breaks for corporations and the wealthiest Americans and restore the Internal Revenue Service’s ability to collect taxes that are already owed. It should also write the Federal Reserve’s independence into law, so that no president can force interest rates down to make government borrowing cheaper. And Congress should establish a bipartisan commission modeled on the 1981 Greenspan Commission, which resolved a Social Security funding crisis, to recommend steps the United States must take to put its finances on a sustainable path and to ensure its global economic competitiveness.

In his 1948 campaign, Harry Truman salvaged his presidency by running against what he called the “do-nothing” Congress. That history should be a warning to Democrats. Voters handed them a congressional majority to bring down costs, and they must start right away to address the forces driving those costs—wars stretching American power to the breaking point, an AI revolution racing beyond human control, and a fiscal hole eroding the foundations of U.S. economic power. If the Democratic majority spends the next two years relitigating the administration’s misdeeds but failing to make progress on the issue voters care most about, Trump and the next Republican presidential candidate will be happy to brand it the do-nothing Congress of 2028.

Sources indicate that passing bills that can become law, forcing the president to veto those that cannot, and using hearings to show Americans what is at stake may still fall short. Ending and averting war, regulating a powerful tech industry, and protecting the United States’ economic competitiveness are difficult for Congress to do without presidential cooperation. But two years without any progress would only leave the affordability problem in place and the United States in a more dangerous global position than it is in now. A Congress that confronts these problems directly can at least make headway. And if it does its job right, it will hand the next president an agenda equal to the moment.

Hakeem Jeffries once called his deep ties to Jerusalem an extension of his representation of New York City as he touted his support for Israel and the Jewish community.

But those comments from 2020, recently resurfaced and going viral, may come back to bite the Democratic House leader as the progressive wing of the party — and even some establishment members — continue to further break with the U.S. maintaining support for the Jewish state.

"Someone said to me, ‘Hakeem, you’re going to Israel a 5th time?’" Jeffries recalled in an interview with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) more than six years ago.

"I said, ‘listen, I’m from Upcoming York City' — and back home in New York City, we consider Jerusalem to be the 6th Borough. And so, I’m just trying to catch up with my constituents.".

The comments resurfaced just after he won his party's nomination to be speaker of the House in the next Congress.

JEFFRIES SURVIVES DEM VOTE TO SECURE SPEAKER POSITION AS PROGRESSIVE RESISTANCE CLOUDS HIS CHANCES.

Sources indicate that minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks before a House vote on funding for the Department of Homeland Security, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on March 5, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images).

The remarks from 2020 contrast starkly with a growing faction of the Democratic Party that has condemned AIPAC and the political favor Israel has historically enjoyed among lawmakers. The clip also raises questions over how far Jeffries will go to placate calls for a more critical review of U.S.-Israel relations in light of his previous support for the Jewish state.

It has been revealed that jeffries won the secret-ballot vote to remain leader of the House’s Democratic Caucus with just 11 in the caucus voting against his leadership and 251 voting in favor. The result secured his nomination ahead of the full House floor vote in January, where he will need a simple majority of the chamber's 435 members to become speaker.

During his AIPAC speech, Jeffries noted that some of his support stemmed from the uniquely challenging geopolitical environment around Israel.

"I think when you’re on the ground, for me it’s always been clear that Israel lives in an incredibly tough neighborhood," Jeffries mentioned.

"When you think about the dangerous situation in the Sinai to the south, Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah to the north, Syria and chaos to the east, Iraq still a mess, Iran with nuclear ambitions and a tremendously bad actor — I grew up in Brooklyn in the late 80s and early 90s, I know from tough neighborhoods that Israel lives in a tough neighborhood," Jeffries stated.

HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL.

In a recent development, the stance clashes forcefully with at least eight members set to be a part of the 120th Congress with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The group aims to "end all military and economic aid to Israel [and] prosecute U.S. and Israeli leaders responsible for the genocide in Gaza.".

Two other members outside of the group, Democratic Reps.-elect Brad Lander and Scott Wiener have similarly called for a full embargo of Israel.

American flags on either side of an Israeli flag (Debbie Hill/Pool/AFP via Getty Images).

Jeffries’ own tone on Israel has changed over the years since the beginning of its war with Hamas in Gaza in October 2023, citing alarm at Israel’s civilian casualties.

In July, Jeffries argued in a letter to his colleagues that "a meaningful change in direction is needed.".

"Israel has an advanced economy and is capable of paying for its own sophisticated weapons, as the Prime Minister recently acknowledged," Jeffries wrote.

"Accordingly, any future security arrangement between our two countries should be structured consistently with defense agreements that exist with our other Western allies and strictly adhere to our human rights laws and values," Jeffries wrote.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., joined by fellow House Democrats, speaks at a press conference outside the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 30, 2025, in Washington, D.C.

"America’s commitment to Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish and democratic state and homeland for the Jewish people must remain ironclad," Jeffries stated in his letter.

In a recent development, protesters rallied outside Hunter College on Nov. 19, 2026, after student leaders scrapped an event featuring Hillel. (#EndJewHatred).

JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, UPCOMING REPORT REVEALS.

"They were establishing a cultural arts night, which I might add also included countries with far worse civil rights violations, like China, and none of that was a problem until, of course, the Jewish organization was involved," noted Shabbos Kestenbaum, who described himself as a Jewish American activist and who works for PragerU.

The USG apologized for sponsoring the event, saying it had "failed" and that the event "should never have moved forward.

The apology remarked the group was actively working to ensure that such a mistake never happened again.

Kestenbaum believes that the school might have run afoul of anti-discrimination laws, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits any entity receiving federal funding from engaging in discrimination based on sex, race, ethnicity or other immutable characteristics.

He advocated for the federal government to pull its funding from Hunter College.

"It's just enforcing the laws already on the books," he noted, adding that President Donald Trump and his administration have been making progress on punishing discriminatory behavior on college campuses.

#65206. Breaking: $275M Obama-era solar fraud case could net taxpayers $1B, but Trump's DOJ backs Biden dismissal

Breaking: $275M Obama-era solar fraud case could net taxpayers $1B, but Trump's DOJ backs Biden dismissal

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, alleges fraud in a $275 million Treasury grant obtained by Crescent Dunes’ former owner and companies linked to Spanish construction giant Cobra.
  • This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada.
  • The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, alleges fraud in a $275 million Treasury grant obtained by Crescent Dunes’ former owner and companies linked to Spanish construction giant Cobra.

This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada. You can read Part 1 here.

The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.

Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why President Donald Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers.

The investors allege that Spanish construction giant ACS and companies to tied its former subsidiary Cobra, misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure.

The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July.

HOW A $1B OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT WENT BANKRUPT TWICE, LEAVING TAXPAYERS WITH THE TAB.

An aerial view of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, highlights thousands of mirrors concentrating sunlight onto the central tower in footage published in 2018. The billion-dollar solar plant later went through two bankruptcies before being sold for $7 million in 2026. (ferrantraite/iStock via Getty Images).

The plant was built around an emerging solar technology that used thousands of mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a towering receiver, heating molten salt that could be stored and used to generate electricity even after sunset.

In 2020, a group of private investors who had put $90 million into the project and suffered substantial losses filed a whistleblower lawsuit, alleging the companies had misled the federal government to secure the enormous grant.

But in November 2024, just two days after Trump's re-election, Biden's Justice Department moved to shut down the lawsuit, arguing that pursuing the case would burden federal agencies.

WHITE HOUSE ROLLS OUT INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD.

Industry observers note that solarReserve, ACS Group/Cobra and Banco Santander were original project participants in Crescent Dunes, which received a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee and approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. CMB investors also provided $90 million in private financing. (Fox News).

DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES.

In a recent development, the incoming Trump administration could have reconsidered that position in early 2025. Instead, its Justice Department defended the Biden-era dismissal in an April filing with a federal appeals court.

CMB, an investment group headed by Pat Hogan, is appealing the dismissal. Hogan is also urging Trump’s Justice Department to ask the court to reopen the case.

"It makes no sense," Hogan told Fox News Digital in a video interview.

Hogan mentioned he had contacted Trump's Justice Department seeking help reviving the case but had received no commitment.

Industry observers note that "The real problem here is, why isn't the government asking for this?" he stated. "All in all, I would say this has just been a fleecing of the federal government by a foreign entity. And we have the opportunity to fix it, and they're doing nothing.".

Hogan argues that allowing the lawsuit to proceed could potentially net hundreds of millions of dollars for taxpayers.

Under the False Claims Act, which CMB used to bring its lawsuit, companies found liable can face damages of up to three times the government's proven losses, plus additional penalties.

"This could be a billion dollars," Hogan mentioned.

According to recent reports, tonopah Solar Energy, the plant's former owner and one of the defendants, has rejected CMB's allegations as baseless in court filings. Other companies named in the lawsuit have also backed the Justice Department's effort to dismiss the case.

Recent findings suggest that in an April 2026 court filing, Trump's Justice Department defended the Biden administration's decision, making the same argument that continuing the lawsuit would drain government resources and that federal law gave it broad authority to shut down the case. In court filings reviewed by Fox News Digital, neither administration put a dollar figure on the cost of continuing the lawsuit.

The decision has left Hogan and his investors questioning why the government shut down the case — and what Treasury officials knew about the plant's serious problems when they approved the $275 million grant.

It has been revealed that pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, whose investors provided $90 million in financing for the Crescent Dunes solar project, is challenging the dismissal of a federal whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving a $275 million Treasury grant. (Provided).

The Crescent Dunes solar plant in Tonopah, Nevada, left, received approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. Private investors allege the plant's former owner and companies involved in its construction fraudulently obtained the funding. The allegations remain disputed, and a federal judge dismissed the whistleblower lawsuit at the Justice Department's request. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital; Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

At the heart of the lawsuit is a dispute over whether Crescent Dunes was properly completed — and whether its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, was entitled to collect the $275 million Treasury grant.

The grant was part of a $26 billion program within the Obama administration's broader $90 billion green-energy push, launched under the 2009 economic stimulus package to create jobs and turbocharge its green energy agenda.

According to recent reports, known as Section 1603, the program paid developers about 30% of their qualifying construction costs once their facilities were "placed in service" — meaning ready and available for their intended use. Treasury considered several factors in determining whether a plant met that standard, including whether it had passed critical tests, begun generating electricity and come under its owner's control.

Crescent Dunes began generating electricity in 2015, but CMB alleges it had produced no more than 32% of its expected output through June 2016.

Then, in October 2016, a failure involving the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank shut it down for months.

A diagram displayed at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, illustrates how thousands of mirrors concentrate sunlight onto a central receiver, heating molten salt that is stored in tanks and used to generate electricity. The diagram bears the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy logo. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

In December, while Crescent Dunes was still shut down, its builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, formally handed the plant over to its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, under an arrangement known as "provisional acceptance.".

But first, they changed the construction contract to allow the handover despite major defects and unfinished repairs.

That agreement came just days before the year-end deadline for solar plants to be ready for use to qualify for the Treasury grants.

According to recent reports, in a later court filing, CMB alleged that more than 9,000 defects had been identified and grouped into roughly 500 outstanding construction items, including seven major deficiencies. The investors argue the problems indicated the plant was not ready to be handed over.

Recent findings suggest that the December agreement itself acknowledged that repairs to the failed hot molten-salt storage tank were still needed. The tank was central to the plant's operation, storing heat from the sun so electricity could be generated even after sunset.

CMB alleges the companies used the revised agreement to make Crescent Dunes appear ready for use and secure the Treasury grant, even though major problems remained unresolved.

Electrical equipment and transmission infrastructure at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

Turbines used in the electricity-generation process sit atop steel infrastructure at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The plant uses heat stored in molten salt to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

Heliostats track the Nevada sun at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah. The mirrors concentrate sunlight onto the receiver atop the tower, visible in the distance. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

Records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Treasury had questioned whether Crescent Dunes was ready for use months before approving the grant payment.

In September 2016, Treasury questioned a claim by Tonopah Solar Energy that Crescent Dunes had been ready for use since February of that year. The agency pointed to a July commissioning report suggesting the builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, had not yet formally handed control of the facility over to Tonopah.

In a Sept. 21 response to Treasury's questions, Tonopah Solar Energy defended its claim, arguing that the plant had passed key tests and was capable of generating electricity. It also acknowledged an earlier extended shutdown caused by problems with the plant's salt-piping system.

The following month, the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank failed, forcing the plant offline for months.

Despite that breakdown, Tonopah and Cobra went ahead with the revised handover agreement in December.

On March 7, 2017, just weeks into the first Trump administration, Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment — even though Crescent Dunes remained shut down nearly five months after the tank failure.

The plant would not resume generating electricity until July 2017.

A timeline shows how Crescent Dunes faced questions over its readiness for operation, suffered a major molten-salt tank failure in October 2016 and remained shut down when Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment in March 2017. An additional $31.9 million was approved in February 2018, bringing total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million. The approvals are central to disputed fraud allegations brought by private investors. (Fox News).

According to recent reports, the hot molten-salt storage tank at Crescent Dunes in Nevada. Repeated leaks involving the plant's molten-salt storage system contributed to lengthy shutdowns and financial troubles. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

A network of pipes and industrial equipment forms part of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The concentrated solar plant uses molten salt to capture and store heat before using it to generate steam and electricity. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

Rows of heliostats converge toward the base of the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. More than 10,000 heliostats surround the tower across the sprawling desert facility. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

According to recent reports, the receiver atop the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project's tower glows as thousands of computer-controlled heliostats concentrate sunlight onto it near Tonopah, Nevada. (Michael Dorgan).

According to recent reports, A view looking up at the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, while the receiver is not being illuminated by concentrated sunlight. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

The approval letter remarked Treasury was still reviewing some of the project's claimed costs before deciding whether to release additional money.

According to recent reports, in February 2018, Treasury approved an additional $31.9 million, bringing the total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million, according to newly obtained federal records. The additional payment was scheduled for disbursement within seven business days.

But Treasury was not the only federal agency involved.

Recent findings suggest that the Department of Energy, which had backed Crescent Dunes with a $737 million federal loan guarantee, also had a say in major construction decisions. DOE approved the revised December handover despite unfinished repairs. It also waived certain missed deadlines, allowing the plant to be formally recognized as operational under its loan agreement.

That approval did not automatically qualify Crescent Dunes for the separate Treasury grant.

A separate December 2016 financing agreement involving Tonopah Solar Energy and DOE required the Treasury grant money to go first toward repaying the project’s short-term federal borrowing, including principal and accrued interest.

Documents obtained by Fox News Digital show that Tonopah Solar Energy made a $218.9 million payment toward a federal loan in March 2017, shortly after Treasury approved its initial grant award.

"So in a sense, the federal government just paid themselves, right? So they're still out the money, right," Hogan told Fox News Digital.

On April 12, 2017, while Crescent Dunes was still offline, DOE published an article celebrating the plant as a breakthrough in solar technology without mentioning that it had been shut down for months.

What remains unclear is whether Treasury officials knew about the October breakdown, unfinished repairs and December contract changes when they authorized the initial grant payment — information that could have affected whether the plant qualified for the grant.

Fox News Digital has asked DOE and Treasury about the grant's approval process, the plant's condition and taxpayer losses, but neither agency has provided a full accounting.

In a statement, the Trump administration's Department of Energy criticized previous administrations' handling of the project, saying it had resolved its financial interests in Crescent Dunes in 2020.

According to recent reports, "It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green New Scam," a DOE spokesperson remarked. "Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project.".

Fox News Digital has also filed Freedom of Information Act requests seeking grant payment records, loan accounting and communications between the agencies.

The Crescent Dunes solar plant near Tonopah, Nevada, features a central tower surrounded by more than 10,000 mirrors that direct sunlight toward a receiver to generate electricity. The Obama-era project, backed by more than $1 billion in federal support, went bankrupt twice before selling for $7 million in July 2026. (Getty Images).

In January 2020, Hogan's investment group, CMB, which had lent $90 million to a tech giant tied to Crescent Dunes developer SolarReserve, sued Tonopah Solar Energy and companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, accusing them of defrauding the federal government.

Industry observers note that the lawsuit was filed under the False Claims Act, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on the government's behalf and receive a share of any money recovered. Known as "qui tam" cases, the lawsuits can be taken over or dismissed by the Justice Department.

After investigating CMB's allegations for more than three years, Biden's Justice Department declined to take over the lawsuit in June 2023, leaving CMB to pursue it alone.

On Nov. 7, 2024, just two days after Trump's election victory, Biden's Justice Department moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that continuing the case would burden the Treasury, Energy and Justice departments.

CMB challenged the move, arguing that Biden's DOJ had failed to explain what had changed since it allowed the investors to proceed.

Then, in July 2025, six months into Trump's second term, a federal judge granted DOJ's request and dismissed the lawsuit without deciding whether the fraud allegations were true.

CMB appealed to the Ninth Circuit, where Trump's Justice Department defended the dismissal in an April 2026 court filing.

Matt Dunn, an attorney at Covington & Burling who specializes in False Claims Act litigation, described DOJ's decision to intervene after initially allowing the case to proceed as "unusual, but not extraordinary.".

Dunn stated the government may have its own assessment of a lawsuit's potential value that differs from the whistleblower's.

"The government might privately have a different view of the merits of the case or the potential value of the case that it doesn't necessarily share publicly," Dunn said.

Dunn said the Supreme Court has given the government substantial discretion to dismiss such cases, describing the legal hurdle for whistleblowers seeking to overturn a dismissal as "an extraordinarily high bar for a relator to overcome.".

Sources indicate that hogan, meanwhile, has a financial stake in the outcome. He claims his investors lost the $90 million they lent to the SolarReserve-linked firm.

If the lawsuit is revived and CMB ultimately succeeds, the government theoretically could recover up to three times its proven damages under the False Claims Act, and CMB could receive a share, potentially offsetting its investors' losses.

"That's my job for my investors to leave no stone unturned to try to make sure that, in fact, I get their money back," Hogan remarked.

The Ninth Circuit must now decide whether the lawsuit can move forward — potentially opening the door for the government to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in disputed funds — or whether DOJ's decision to shut it down will stand.

The Justice Department's handling of the case has also drawn scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

Industry observers note that in February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit.

Gooden later urged Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to consider suspending federal contracts with companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, whose subsidiary Cobra built the plant and held a stake in Tonopah Solar Energy. He also called for an investigation into ACS and Banco Santander's roles in the project's financing and bankruptcy amid the allegations of fraud involving federal funds.

"When taxpayers are defrauded to a scale this massive, our government has a responsibility to get the facts and hold those responsible to account," Gooden told Fox News Digital. "That is why I have asked Secretary Hegseth to pause contracts with ACS-affiliated entities until these allegations are fully reviewed and every avenue to recover taxpayer money has been pursued.".

In February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

Rep. Carol Miller, R-W.Va., leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 29, 2023. Miller has questioned the collapse of the federally backed Crescent Dunes solar plant and the potential loss of taxpayer money. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images).

Industry observers note that one such contract involves a $2.84 billion Navy dry dock project at Pearl Harbor awarded to a joint venture involving ACS subsidiary Dragados. The project completion date has been delayed from September 2027 to March 2029, according to the Government Accountability Office. Dragados is not accused of fraud in the Crescent Dunes lawsuit.

Miller, meanwhile, also questioned how a project backed by nearly $1 billion in federal financing could end up selling for $7 million.

"That's not good math," Miller told Fox News Digital. She suggested another congressional letter could be warranted, saying that "if we can recover any of that taxpayer money, that would be wonderful.".

In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead.

In a July 10 response obtained by Fox News Digital, DOJ revealed that Crescent Dunes was one of just 12 cases in which it moved to shut down a lawsuit after initially allowing it to proceed — fewer than 0.3% of nearly 5,000 whistleblower cases received between 2020 and 2025.

It has been revealed that DOJ also confirmed that other federal agencies can push to have such lawsuits dismissed, including to avoid the burden of producing evidence. But it did not say whether Treasury or DOE pushed to kill the Crescent Dunes case — or what investigators found when they examined the fraud allegations.

Recent findings suggest that in April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

The companies accused of fraud have backed DOJ's effort to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that federal law gives the government broad authority to shut down whistleblower cases.

Tonopah Solar Energy, which filed for bankruptcy in January 2026, has also fiercely rejected CMB's allegations, accusing the investors of pursuing a "scorched earth mission" through repeated legal challenges against the company.

"The reality is there is no merit to CMB's claims whatsoever," the tech giant argued in an April 2026 bankruptcy filing.

According to recent reports, tonopah Solar Energy made those arguments while winding down its affairs in bankruptcy, before selling the plant's assets in July. The new owners had no involvement in the alleged 2016 fraud, and the bankruptcy sale generally shielded them from the former owner's legal liabilities.

In a separate 2020 lawsuit, Hogan's investors sought to recover an allegedly unpaid $90 million loan, suing companies tied to Crescent Dunes after SolarReserve failed to repay much of the money. They suffered a setback in 2024 when an arbitration panel rejected five of their claims and ordered them to pay $2.44 million in legal fees and costs.

The companies did not respond to Fox News Digital's repeated requests for comment.

The dispute was separate from the whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving the $275 million Treasury grant.

Despite years of investigation, the Justice Department has never publicly disclosed what it uncovered.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

Nearly seven years after Hogan's investors filed their lawsuit, the fraud allegations have never been tested at trial. And despite President Trump's pledge to crack down on fraud and wasteful green-energy spending, his Justice Department is still defending the Biden administration's decision to shut down the case.

Industry observers note that "If we're wrong, the evidence will show it," Hogan remarked. "But don't let a Biden-era dismissal prevent the merits from ever being heard.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow at the Heritage Foundation, tells Fox News Digital that Gov. Gavin Newsom may be imposing his own views of the death penalty over those of other Californians.

Recent findings suggest that A lawsuit challenging Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute 548 death sentences is raising questions about the governor's clemency powers, with a legal expert arguing Newsom is using his gubernatorial authority to circumvent the will of voters who have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish capital punishment.

Sources indicate that newsom declared Nov. 5 that he intends to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the Golden State's death row to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that will take effect only after the necessary legal steps are completed.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF) on Sunday filed a lawsuit at the California Supreme Court seeking to block Newsom's proposed sweeping commutation, citing the governor's "failure to provide legally required notice to district attorneys and his disregard for the rights of victims and their families to be notified and heard," according to a news release.

Newsom may be using clemency to impose his own views on capital punishment despite voters repeatedly rejecting abolition, Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for Courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATED FOR NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom takes questions from the media. (Reuters/Fred Greaves).

"The death penalty remains on the books in California, and as you alluded to, California voters have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish the death penalty," Smith said. "So Californians understand that it can be an appropriate punishment in certain circumstances. Now, [Gov.] Newsom, he does have the ability to exercise the pardon, the commutation power, the contours of that obviously are being litigated, but I think what's clear is that from a practical standpoint, [Gov.] Newsom is essentially using this to circumvent the clear will of the voters and impose his own views of the death penalty over those of ... the California populace.".

Recent findings suggest that "Now some of the specifics related to this suit challenging Gavin Newsom's use of the commutation pardon, that is going to vary a little bit from state to state," Smith added. "So this is going focus largely on concerns of California state law and the issues specifically that I think will get the most attention is whether the California Supreme Court would essentially have to weigh in and more or less approve some of these repeat offenders before their sentences can be commuted.".

Recent findings suggest that california voters notably defeated Proposition 34, a ballot initiative to ban capital punishment, in 2012, according to Ballotpedia. Voters in the Golden State similarly rejected Proposition 62, the Abolition of Death Penalty Measure, in November 2016, per Ballotpedia.

The lawsuit alleges that Newsom "has claimed to himself the unfettered power to decide how clemency should be granted, ignored the Legislature’s requirement of a referral to the Board of Parole Hearings for investigation and recommendation, ignored the role of the trial court and District Attorney in providing crucial factual input to the Board of Parole Hearings, ignored the limitation of the required notice to District Attorneys, and deprived the Legislature, the public, and this Court of the information needed to determine whether he has abused his authority.".

CJLF's lawsuit also requests that "the Court immediately stay any issuance, implementation, recognition, or enforcement of the challenged commutations pending further order of the Court and pending determination of this petition on the merits.".

Anne Marie Schubert, president and CEO of CJLF, said in a statement that the lawsuit "is about protecting the constitutional rights of victims, defending the rule of law, and ensuring that no Governor is above the law.".

"The Governor’s clemency power does not authorize mass commutations that disregard constitutional safeguards, legally required procedures, or victims’ rights," Schubert stated, adding that "blanket commutation is not an exercise of discretion — it is an abandonment of it.".

CJLF and Newsom's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The coalition suing Newsom is comprised of several law enforcement leaders and organizations, victims’ rights groups and multiple district attorneys, including Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho, who ran as a Democrat in the 2026 congressional primary.

Some of California’s most notorious serial killers are among the death row inmates whose sentences Newsom intends to commute, KTLA reported Nov. 8.

"Obviously, these are individuals who, again, have been convicted by a jury of their peers of committing particularly aggravated forms of murder," Smith told Fox News Digital. "Again, many of these individuals tortured their victims and included sexual violence against their victims before they were ultimately killed. And so these are individuals that their own peers thought deserved the death penalty. And, so again, to see [Gov.] Newsom circumventing this through his commutation power is very, very troubling.".

Under the California Constitution, Newsom must obtain a recommendation from at least four California Supreme Court justices before commuting the sentences of 382 inmates who have been convicted of more than one felony.

Sources indicate that the California Supreme Court has invited interested parties to weigh in on the proposed commutations, with legal briefs due Nov. 24 and Newsom's response due Dec. 4. Attorney General Rob Bonta told the court Newsom will not formally commute any death sentences until the justices act, including those of inmates with only one felony conviction.

Newsom's office has argued that the governor's broad constitutional clemency authority allows him to initiate blanket commutations without following statutory procedures governing individual applications, while separately seeking the California Supreme Court's required recommendation for inmates with multiple felony convictions.

This week, Soneil Spark rolls out its Mobile Battery Energy Storage System (Mobile BESS), the portable, modular battery storage built into a towable trailer.

The company, offering bespoke, modular energy solutions, is introducing Mobile BESS at RE+ 2026. It delivers temporary backup and off-grid power, working with what’s available by taking power from the grid, a generator, or solar.

“Wherever your business goes, the power goes with it. Simply tow it where energy demand grows,” mentioned Sonya Jain, CEO of Soneil Spark, in a statement. “Start with one unit and add more as your needs change.”.

It’s a simple set up, the company mentioned. Mobile BESS works with no crane, no trenching, and no utility wait. That makes it a natural fit for a job site which may be months away from permanent service, a film set or event that can’t tolerate generator noise and fumes, a utility crew restoring power after a storm, or a remote mine or farm beyond the grid’s reach.

Sources indicate that on sites that already run generators, the Mobile BESS syncs with them to cover peaks and start-up gaps, so the generators run fewer hours. Where diesel is restricted, it offers a quiet alternative.

Industry observers note that where containerized storage is built to be placed once, the Mobile BESS is built to be towed and to work in any weather. It includes:.

The Mobile BESS is built for generator and equipment rental, construction, emergency and backup power, utilities, electrical contractors, events, film and entertainment, and off-grid sites such as mining and agriculture. A hybrid option adds EV charging.

#65201. A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Npr ↗ Open Full Page

A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Npr

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Trump holds up a model of his proposed triumphal arch at a White House event in Oct.
  • A federal judge in Virginia prepares to concern a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.
  • District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Trump holds up a model of his proposed triumphal arch at a White House event in Oct. 2025. Two different federal judges have ruled against it this week. John McDonnell/AP hide caption.

A federal judge in Virginia prepares to concern a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.

District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.

"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.

Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.

Sources indicate that the 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.

Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it stated an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.

Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.

In a recent development, "In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services.".

The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and remarked building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.

"The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.

NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.".

Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.

On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.

It has been revealed that that case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.

Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.

And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge noted in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.

She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.

"It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.

Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has stated would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.

It has been revealed that the Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.
